home.traceTitle: What was running at the same time
home.traceLede: One time axis; each bar is a system, a job or a programme. Where they overlap is where they were running together — the part a list cannot show and this cannot hide. Drag to pan, scroll to zoom; wherever the pointer sits, the readout says how many were running that day.
home.traceSource: Every bar's dates are quoted from the case study it links to — the sources are recorded in content/periods.ts, each naming the sentence it was read from, and a project with no stated dates gets no bar at all. Bars that fade at the edges are known only to the year or the month. The four figures below are computed from the same spans, not typed.
home.workLede: Each row carries its own slice of the axis above it. The short red line under a name is the time that system took.
home.rulesLede: Not principles read somewhere. Each came from one specific thing, caught in acceptance or in the week before launch. They are written as rules rather than as virtues, because a virtue is not evidence of anything.

about.title: About
about.p1: I'm binbin — still a student, and since June 2025 a full-stack developer at Manience Inc., where I build the AI nail platform and the dozens of Django microservices behind it.
about.p2: During acceptance on the HR system I found that the payroll API cached without the user in the key — inside one TTL window an employee would hit an admin’s cached response and see company-wide salaries. It threw no error, it was not slow, the tests were green. That is when I started believing that cache design is authorization design.
